svg.title: DDIA 5 · REPLICATION: sketchnote
svg.text: Keep a copy of the same data on several machines: for fault tolerance (a node dies,
a copy survives), read scaling (spread reads), and latency (a copy near the user).
Reads can go to any follower. This is read scaling, but
followers may be a little behind: replication lag.
The async follower is updated in the background. It is fast,
but if the leader dies now, writes the async follower never got
SPLIT BRAIN → two leaders accept writes
If the old leader returns and still thinks it is leader, there are
two leaders: split brain. A fix is fencing: shut it down
HOW THE REPLICATION LOG IS IMPLEMENTED
Exact copy, but tied to the
must run the same DB version
Fix: read own data from leader
The fixes give read-after-write consistency: read the user's
own profile from the leader; for about 1 minute after a write,
route that user to the leader; or have the client remember its
last write LSN and read only from a replica that has caught up
Consistent prefix: answer seen before the question
Consistent prefix reads: across partitions a reader can see a
reply before the message it replies to.
When the changes meet, there is a conflict. Resolution options:
last-write-wins (silently loses data), merge values, CRDTs, or
Read repair writes the latest value back to the stale node. A
background anti-entropy process (Merkle trees) fixes values
Automated failover promotes a replica (Patroni, RDS Multi-AZ,
"User updates a price and refreshes but sees the old price."
Replication lag. Read-your-writes: route that user to the
primary for N seconds, or track LSN.
Multi-leader with conflict risk. Prefer a home region per user or
hotel, and CRDTs for things like counters.
Leaderless: no failover pause, tunable consistency, write
availability during node loss. The cost is conflicts and LWW.
Study notes on Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann). Read the book.
